metadata.file_name: 2. Zhu et al. (2025). Predictive insights into U.S. students’ mathematics performance on PISA 2022 using ensemble tree-based machine learning models.pdf
metadata.title: Predictive insights into U.S. students’ mathematics performance on PISA 2022 using ensemble tree-based machine learning models

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2022 microdata for the United States and merges student and school files using the school ID (CNTSCHID), assigning school-level predictors to students within the same school. The analytic dataset contains 4552 students in 154 schools, with grade filtering implicitly reflected in the reported grade distribution (mostly 10th grade). The authors explicitly did not include sampling weights in the ML analyses, citing that weighting might be less critical for ML model configuration and that ML can still produce reliable results without incorporating sampling weights under complex multistage clustered designs. Data preparation included removing predictors with >50% missingness, deleting identical and redundant predictors (e.g., excluding components used to compute ESCS), and imputing remaining missing predictor values using RF-based missForest before splitting into training (80%) and test (20%) sets.

data.outcome_summary: The study predicts U.S. students’ PISA 2022 mathematics performance using ensemble tree-based ML models (Random Forest, XGBoost, LightGBM) trained separately for each of the 10 math plausible values (PV1MATH–PV10MATH). After cleaning and RF-based missForest imputation, the authors select influential predictors using an absolute relative error (ARE) criterion (ARE < 0.1) and compare reduced models to full models using root mean squared error (rMSE) and training time. Model comparison shows XGBoost as best overall: reduced-model rMSE = 66.39 with 10 predictors and training time = 4.14 s, outperforming LightGBM (rMSE = 66.36; 22.93 s) and Random Forest (rMSE = 69.82; 129.27 s). Across all three ML models, the top shared predictors are MATHEFF (math self-efficacy), ESCS (socioeconomic status), FAMCON (familiarity with math concepts), BSMJ (expected occupation status), and FAMSUPSL (family support for self-directed learning). Using ALE plots for XGBoost, MATHEFF and ESCS show positive associations with math performance, while several opportunity/propensity-related predictors (e.g., WORKPAY, EXERPRAC, FEELLAH, ANXMAT at higher levels) show negative or non-linear effects; the authors note ML interpretability via ALE but do not claim causal effects.
